notation.meaning: Effective minimum: log minimum minus log median (or trimmed mean)
Log wage at percentile $p$ in state $j$ (or $s$), year $t$
Log real minimum wage in state $s$, year $t$
Trimmed mean of log wages, 30th–70th percentiles
Measurement error in the log wage at percentile $p$

blocks.md: **The previous lecture asked what minimum wages do to employment; this one asks what they do to inequality. The real federal minimum fell every year from 1979 to 1989, exactly as inequality rose. DiNardo, Fortin and Lemieux show it in the wage densities; Lee uses the fact that one federal minimum bites harder in low-wage states, and finds it explains all of the rise at the bottom — suspiciously, also some at the top. Autor, Manning and Smith show the top-tail effect is a measurement-error artefact; instrumented, the falling minimum explains about half of the rise in women's lower-tail inequality and a tenth of men's. Brazil, which raised its minimum 128%, shows the same approach at scale, and Vogel brings the minimum back into the race between education and technology.**

blocks.title: Sources and notation
blocks.md: This summary follows the slides of Jonathan Vogel's lecture; slides marked "Skip" are summarized briefly. All wages are in logs. $w^{p}$ is the log wage at percentile $p$; "10-50" is $w^{10} - w^{50}$, the negative of the 50/10 log gap ([Percentile Ratios](note:percentile-ratios)). The **effective minimum wage** $mw$ is the log minimum minus the log median (or trimmed mean) of a state's wages ([Effective Minimum Wage](note:effective-minimum-wage)).

What happens to inequality when the minimum wage falls? The real value of the federal minimum fell in every year between 1979 and 1989 — from about 7 to about 5.2 (2012 dollars, chart-read) — exactly coinciding with the large rise in inequality ([US Minimum Wage and Lower-Tail Wage Inequality 1979-2012](note:us-minimum-wage-and-lower-tail-wage-inequality-1979-2012)).

blocks.src: assets/Attachments/US real federal minimum wage 1979-2012.png
blocks.alt: US real federal minimum wage 1979-2012
blocks.caption: The federal minimum was not raised between 1981 and 1990, so inflation eroded it every year.

sections.heading: 2. DiNardo, Fortin and Lemieux (1996): the picture

blocks.md: DFL plot kernel-density estimates of real log hourly wages ([Kernel Density Estimation](note:kernel-density-estimation)) from the CPS for each year, with the real minimum marked. In the 1970s there is a spike at the minimum; from 1979 the minimum falls in real terms, the spike drifts left and fades, and the lower tail spreads out. Somewhat clear for men, incredibly clear for women.

blocks.src: assets/Attachments/DiNardo, Fortin and Lemieux 1996 - densities of men's log wages 1973-1992.png
blocks.alt: DiNardo, Fortin and Lemieux 1996 - densities of men's log wages 1973-1992

blocks.src: assets/Attachments/DiNardo, Fortin and Lemieux 1996 - densities of women's log wages 1973-1992.png
blocks.alt: DiNardo, Fortin and Lemieux 1996 - densities of women's log wages 1973-1992

blocks.md: They then conduct a statistical (accounting) decomposition of the importance of supply, demand, the federal minimum and unionization for the wage distribution, asking: *what would the density of wages have been if individual attributes had remained at their year $t$ level and workers had been paid according to the wage schedule of year $t'$?* For the minimum wage the idea is simple: superimpose the 1979 real minimum on the 1988 density, keep the same mass to the left of it as in 1979, and move the rest up to the minimum ([DiNardo-Fortin-Lemieux Reweighting](note:dinardo-fortin-lemieux-reweighting)).

blocks.src: assets/Attachments/DiNardo, Fortin and Lemieux 1996 - adjusting the 1988 distribution to the 1979 minimum wage.png
blocks.alt: DiNardo, Fortin and Lemieux 1996 - adjusting the 1988 distribution to the 1979 minimum wage

blocks.prompt: DFL build a counterfactual 1988 wage density "with the 1979 real minimum wage". Which assumption does that counterfactual require?

options.md: Workers paid below the 1979 minimum lose their jobs
options.feedback: The opposite: the counterfactual moves them up to the minimum, keeping everyone employed.

options.md: The minimum affects only wages below it, and has no employment effects
Wages above the minimum rise by the same amount as wages at the minimum
options.feedback: That would be large spillovers; the counterfactual leaves wages above the minimum unchanged.

options.md: The minimum wage was randomly assigned across states
options.feedback: DFL use national data over time, not state variation; that is Lee's idea.

blocks.why: The reweighting simply piles the mass below the old minimum at the minimum and leaves the rest of the distribution untouched. It is an accounting exercise built on those assumptions, so it does not give a causal answer. The takeaway: clear graphical evidence that the minimum wage and the wage distribution are related.

blocks.md: Paper summary: [DiNardo, Fortin and Lemieux 1996 - Labor Market Institutions and the Distribution of Wages](note:dinardo-fortin-and-lemieux-1996-labor-market-institutions-and-the-distribution-of-wages)

Lee asks whether the federal minimum affects the wage distribution, and how much its decline contributed to inequality. His motivation repeats DFL: densities for men, women and everyone, 1979 versus 1989, and percentiles relative to the median, which fell at the bottom as the minimum fell relative to the median.

blocks.src: assets/Attachments/Lee 1999 - wage densities for all workers 1979 and 1989.png
blocks.alt: Lee 1999 - wage densities for all workers 1979 and 1989

blocks.src: assets/Attachments/Lee 1999 - wage percentiles and the minimum wage relative to the median 1973-1993.png
blocks.alt: Lee 1999 - wage percentiles and the minimum wage relative to the median 1973-1993
blocks.caption: All series are 0 in 1979. By 1989 the minimum had fallen about 0.38 log points relative to the median, the 10th percentile about 0.14 (chart-read).

blocks.md: His approach exploits the spatial variation: **(1)** state incomes differ a lot, so with the same national minimum it binds more in a low-income state (the primary variation); **(2)** some states set their own minimum above the federal one, so with the same income it binds more there (secondary — there was little of it in his period). In high- versus low-wage states the 10-50 gap evolved very differently, while the 75-50 gap evolved almost identically.

blocks.src: assets/Attachments/Lee 1999 - 10-50 and 75-50 differentials in high- and low-wage states.png
blocks.alt: Lee 1999 - 10-50 and 75-50 differentials in high- and low-wage states

blocks.src: assets/Attachments/Lee 1999 - wage densities in low-, medium- and high-wage states 1979.png
blocks.alt: Lee 1999 - wage densities in low-, medium- and high-wage states 1979
blocks.caption: In 1979, a spatial version of DFL's figures: the minimum sits much further into the distribution of low-wage states.

blocks.md: Why states, not education groups? Variation across states comes closest to the ideal experiment of randomly allocating minimum wages across labor markets, and by the late 1980s there is some variation in state-legislated minimums. The data are the CPS outgoing rotation groups (MORG).

blocks.src: assets/Attachments/Lee 1999 - 10-50 differential vs relative minimum wage across states.png
blocks.alt: Lee 1999 - 10-50 differential vs relative minimum wage across states
blocks.caption: In 1979, when the minimum bound, the gap between the minimum and the median tracks the 10-50 gap almost linearly across states; in 1989 they are unrelated except where the minimum is close to the median.

blocks.md: **Estimation.** With all wages in logs, Lee regresses

blocks.tex: w^{10}_{jt} - w^{50}_{jt} = \alpha_t + \beta\, mw_{jt} + \gamma\, mw_{jt}^2 + u_{jt}, \qquad mw_{jt} \equiv \text{min wage}_t - w^{50}_{jt}

blocks.md: with year dummies $\alpha_t$. The key identifying assumption is that the distribution of **latent** wages — the distribution in the absence of the minimum — is common across space. Because the median enters both sides, measurement error in it generates endogeneity; his final specification replaces the median with a trimmed mean $\bar{w}_{jt}$ of the middle of the distribution.

blocks.prompt: What does Lee's key identifying assumption say?

options.md: Without the minimum wage, every state's wage distribution (relative to its center) would have the same shape
The minimum wage is set independently of each state's median wage
options.feedback: The federal minimum is common to all states; what varies is how it compares with each state's wages.

options.md: The minimum wage has no effect on employment
options.feedback: That is an assumption of DFL's counterfactual, not the one that identifies Lee's regression.

options.md: Wage inequality is the same in every state
options.feedback: Observed inequality differs across states — that is the variation he uses. The assumption is about the *latent* distribution.

blocks.why: If latent distributions share a shape, then differences across states in the lower tail can only come from where the minimum sits relative to each state's center. A low-wage state then shows us what a high-wage state's distribution would look like with a more binding minimum.

blocks.src: assets/Attachments/Table - Lee 1999 10-50 differential on the minimum wage.png
blocks.alt: Table - Lee 1999 10-50 differential on the minimum wage

blocks.md: With the trimmed mean, $\beta = 1.494$ and $\gamma = 0.634$: the marginal effect of the effective minimum on the 10-50 gap is $\beta + 2\gamma\, mw$, which depends on how close the minimum is to the center of the distribution.

blocks.prompt: Predict how much the 10-50 gap responds at the average effective minimum

predict.ask: Lee estimates $\beta = 1.494$ and $\gamma = 0.634$. At the average effective minimum, $mw = -0.77$, by how much does the 10-50 log wage gap change when the effective minimum rises by one log point?

blocks.md: The marginal effect is $1.494 + 2(0.634)(-0.77) = 0.52$ (Lee reports 0.515): about half of a rise in the minimum passes into the 10th percentile relative to the center. It is 0.86 when the minimum is close to the median ($mw = -0.5$) and zero once the minimum falls about 1.18 log points below it — so a falling real minimum moves low-wage states down a steep part of this curve.

blocks.prompt: Drag the effective minimum and find where it stops biting

goal.success: At $mw = -1.18$, $\beta + 2\gamma\, mw = 0$: a minimum this far below the center of the distribution no longer moves its bottom tail. In 1979 many low-wage states were near $-0.5$, where the effect is 0.86; the falling real minimum pushed them toward this point.
goal.hint: Drag the point left, toward a minimum further below the median, and watch the effect fall.

blocks.src: assets/Attachments/Table - Lee 1999 upper-tail differentials on the minimum wage.png
blocks.alt: Table - Lee 1999 upper-tail differentials on the minimum wage

blocks.md: The same regression for upper-tail gaps finds no effect on the 60-50, but for men "quite an effect" on the 70-50, 80-50 and 90-50 gaps — a minimum wage should not move wages at the 90th percentile. Lee's interpretation: perhaps we should focus more on the results for women.

*(Skip slides.)* An alternative approach compares states whose own minimum was above the new federal one with states that were bound by it when the federal minimum rose in 1990–91; and counterfactual distributions for 1989 with each state's 1979 effective minimum, $\Delta p_{j,89} = \hat\beta_p(mw_{j,79} - mw_{j,89}) + \hat\gamma_p(mw_{j,79}^2 - mw_{j,89}^2)$.

blocks.src: assets/Attachments/Lee 1999 - actual and latent changes in wage percentiles 1979-1989.png
blocks.alt: Lee 1999 - actual and latent changes in wage percentiles 1979-1989

blocks.md: **Summary:** changes in the minimum can explain all (!) of the change in inequality at the bottom. Perhaps it does too well, especially at the top of the distribution for men. What is the cause of this over-abundance of success — and should it make us skeptical overall?
Paper summary: [Lee 1999 - Wage Inequality in the US During the 1980s](note:lee-1999-wage-inequality-in-the-us-during-the-1980s)

sections.heading: 4. Autor, Manning and Smith (2016): a reassessment

blocks.md: AMS revisit Lee with (1) two more decades of data, in which state minimums vary a lot more, and (2) an instrumental-variables strategy that addresses the bias. They also use the CPS MORG.

blocks.src: assets/Attachments/Table - Autor, Manning and Smith 2016 bindingness of minimum wages.png
blocks.alt: Table - Autor, Manning and Smith 2016 bindingness of minimum wages

blocks.src: assets/Attachments/Autor, Manning and Smith 2016 - share of hours at or below the minimum wage.png
blocks.alt: Autor, Manning and Smith 2016 - share of hours at or below the minimum wage
blocks.caption: Share of hours at or below the minimum: high for women in 1979 (about 13%), much lower for men (about 5%).

blocks.md: Their baseline, for any percentile $p$ in state $s$ and year $t$:

with state effects $\sigma_{s0}(p)$, state trends $\sigma_{s1}(p)$ and year effects $\gamma_t(p)$. Estimated by OLS, the results look a lot like Lee's: significant effects on the lower tail, but also on the upper tail. True effect, or bias?

blocks.src: assets/Attachments/Autor, Manning and Smith 2016 - OLS marginal effects by percentile.png
blocks.alt: Autor, Manning and Smith 2016 - OLS marginal effects by percentile

blocks.md: **The bias.** Suppose $w_{st}(p)$ is measured with error $\varepsilon^\mu_{st}(p)$, and errors at nearby percentiles are more correlated ([Classical Measurement Error](note:classical-measurement-error)). The explanatory variable contains $-\varepsilon^\mu_{st}(50)$; the dependent variable, and so the residual, contains $\varepsilon^\mu_{st}(p) - \varepsilon^\mu_{st}(50)$. Both contain the median's error, so they are correlated — weakly near $p = 50$, where the two errors nearly cancel, and strongly far from it.

blocks.prompt: In AMS's OLS regressions the minimum wage appears to affect the 90-50 gap. Why might that be spurious?

options.md: A wrongly measured median enters both sides of the regression, making the 90-50 gap and the effective minimum move together
The minimum wage spills over to high earners through the job ladder
options.feedback: That would be a true effect; AMS find it disappears once the bias is removed.

options.md: The 90th percentile is measured with less error than the median
options.feedback: The problem is the median's error, which appears in both variables whatever the error at the 90th.

options.md: State fixed effects absorb the true effect at the top
options.feedback: Fixed effects are in both the OLS and the IV specifications; only the IV removes the upper-tail effect.

blocks.why: If the median is measured too high, the effective minimum $w^m - w(50)$ is too low and the gap $w(90) - w(50)$ is too small at the same time, so they move together even with no true effect. The bias grows with the distance from the 50th percentile, exactly where an effect is least plausible.

blocks.md: **Instrument.** An instrument must be correlated with the endogenous explanatory variables and uncorrelated with the error ([Instrumental Variables and 2SLS](note:instrumental-variables-and-2sls)). Since the endogeneity comes from the median being on both sides, AMS instrument with the log real minimum wage, its square, and the log real minimum times the state's average median wage over the full sample.

blocks.src: assets/Attachments/Table - Autor, Manning and Smith 2016 OLS and 2SLS by gender.png
blocks.alt: Table - Autor, Manning and Smith 2016 OLS and 2SLS by gender

blocks.src: assets/Attachments/Autor, Manning and Smith 2016 - 2SLS marginal effects by percentile.png
blocks.alt: Autor, Manning and Smith 2016 - 2SLS marginal effects by percentile

blocks.md: Instrumented, the effects are smaller at the bottom, extend only to the 20th percentile for women and the 5th (or 10th) for men, and vanish at the top. Running Lee's specification on their extended data shows the differences come both from the longer sample and from the instrument.

blocks.src: assets/Attachments/Autor, Manning and Smith 2016 - Lee specification on the extended data.png
blocks.alt: Autor, Manning and Smith 2016 - Lee specification on the extended data

blocks.md: *(Skip slides.)* How much of the rise in lower-tail inequality since 1979 can the declining minimum explain? Following Lee, AMS adjust each wage by $\hat\beta_1(\tilde{m}_{s,\tau_0} - \tilde{m}_{s,\tau_1}) + \hat\beta_2(\tilde{m}^2_{s,\tau_0} - \tilde{m}^2_{s,\tau_1})$ to hold the effective minimum at its starting level.

blocks.src: assets/Attachments/Table - Autor, Manning and Smith 2016 actual and counterfactual changes in 50-10.png
blocks.alt: Table - Autor, Manning and Smith 2016 actual and counterfactual changes in 50-10

blocks.prompt: In AMS's Table 3, women's log 50/10 gap rose 28.5 log points from 1979 to 2012; holding the effective minimum constant (2SLS), it would have risen 14.8. What share of the rise does the declining minimum explain? Give a percentage.

wrong.md: that is the counterfactual's share of the rise; the minimum explains the rest, $28.5 - 14.8$
that is the explained rise in log points; divide by the observed rise
that divides the explained rise by the counterfactual; divide by the observed rise, 28.5

blocks.why: $(28.5 - 14.8)/28.5 = 0.48$: about half. For men, $(7.9 - 7.0)/7.9 = 11\%$; pooled, 39%. Lee's approach attributes essentially all of it.

blocks.src: assets/Attachments/Autor, Manning and Smith 2016 - actual and counterfactual changes by percentile.png
blocks.alt: Autor, Manning and Smith 2016 - actual and counterfactual changes by percentile

blocks.md: **Summary:** with OLS, AMS find results that look a lot like Lee's, but the approach has an endogeneity problem. With a reasonable instrument, effects are smaller at the bottom and absent at the top. The fall in the minimum wage in the 1980s explains none of the growth of upper-tail inequality, and about 10% (men) and 50% (women) of the growth of lower-tail inequality. *(The slide attributes these shares to the 1980s; in AMS's Table 3 they are the 1979–2012 shares — for 1979–89 alone the 2SLS shares are about half for both.)*

Paper summary: [Autor, Manning and Smith 2016 - The Contribution of the Minimum Wage to US Wage Inequality](note:autor-manning-and-smith-2016-the-contribution-of-the-minimum-wage-to-us-wage-inequality)

Brazil is a test where minimum-wage changes were larger and more persistent: between 1996 and 2018 it raised the real minimum by 128%. Engbom and Moser follow Lee's and AMS's approaches with administrative data ([Brazil Minimum Wage and Earnings Inequality 1996-2018](note:brazil-minimum-wage-and-earnings-inequality-1996-2018)).

blocks.src: assets/Attachments/Engbom and Moser 2022 - real minimum wage and earnings inequality in Brazil.png
blocks.alt: Engbom and Moser 2022 - real minimum wage and earnings inequality in Brazil
blocks.caption: The standard deviation of log earnings fell as the real minimum rose.

blocks.src: assets/Attachments/Engbom and Moser 2022 - Brazil wage distributions and percentile ratios.png
blocks.alt: Engbom and Moser 2022 - Brazil wage distributions and percentile ratios

blocks.src: assets/Attachments/Engbom and Moser 2022 - inequality in high- and low-income Brazilian states.png
blocks.alt: Engbom and Moser 2022 - inequality in high- and low-income Brazilian states
blocks.caption: Inequality fell much more in low-income states, where the national minimum bites hardest — Lee's spatial variation.

blocks.src: assets/Attachments/Engbom and Moser 2022 - minimum wage effects by percentile.png
blocks.alt: Engbom and Moser 2022 - minimum wage effects by percentile

blocks.md: Baseline regressions in levels (OLS; IV is similar here): relative to the median, effects are large at the bottom and fade to zero by the median; relative to the 90th percentile they stay positive up to about the 80th — spillovers reach further up than in the US.

blocks.prompt: Brazil's lowest-income states saw much larger falls in lower-tail inequality than its richest states as the national minimum rose. Why is that the pattern the minimum-wage explanation predicts?

options.md: The same national minimum is closer to typical pay in a low-income state, so it compresses more of its distribution
Low-income states set their own, higher minimum wages
options.feedback: Brazil's minimum is national; the variation comes from how it compares with local wages.

options.md: Workers moved from low- to high-income states
options.feedback: Migration would not produce larger compression in the states people leave.

options.md: High-income states have more college workers
options.feedback: That affects upper-tail inequality, not where the minimum binds.

blocks.why: A higher effective minimum (closer to the median) means a larger marginal effect, $\beta + 2\gamma\, mw$. A uniform national minimum therefore bites hardest in poor states — the identifying variation in Lee and AMS, at a much larger scale.

blocks.md: Paper summary: [Engbom and Moser 2022 - Earnings Inequality and the Minimum Wage](note:engbom-and-moser-2022-earnings-inequality-and-the-minimum-wage)

sections.heading: 6. Back to macro inequality: the college premium

blocks.md: Autor, Katz and Kearney (2008) estimate the canonical supply–demand model of the college/high-school wage gap for 1963–2005 ([Canonical Model of the Skill Premium](note:canonical-model-of-the-skill-premium)). Adding the log real (federal) minimum wage barely changes the relative supply coefficient, and the minimum's coefficient is small and imprecise: institutions do not resolve the puzzle of slowing trend demand for college workers after 1992.

blocks.src: assets/Attachments/Table - Autor, Katz and Kearney 2008 college premium regressions.png
blocks.alt: Table - Autor, Katz and Kearney 2008 college premium regressions

blocks.md: Paper summary: [Autor, Katz and Kearney 2008 - Trends in US Wage Inequality](note:autor-katz-and-kearney-2008-trends-in-us-wage-inequality)

Vogel (2025) argues that AKK (1) measured the real minimum with the federal version, not state minimums, and (2) had a short time horizon. **Result 1:** with more data (1963–2016) and state minimums, conclusions change. The real minimum enters with an elasticity of −0.13 to −0.22, depending on the time polynomial, while relative supply stays around −0.6.

blocks.src: assets/Attachments/Vogel 2025 - residualized college premium, supply and minimum wage.png
blocks.alt: Vogel 2025 - residualized college premium, supply and minimum wage

blocks.src: assets/Attachments/Table - Vogel 2025 college premium regressions with the minimum wage.png
blocks.alt: Table - Vogel 2025 college premium regressions with the minimum wage

blocks.prompt: The real minimum wage fell by about 26% between 1979 and 1989. If the college premium's elasticity to the real minimum is −0.13 in Vogel's estimates, so that its absolute value is $\varepsilon = 0.13$, by how much did that raise the college premium? Give a percentage with one decimal.

wrongCompute.md: multiply the percentage change by the elasticity
the elasticity scales the change: multiply, don't divide

blocks.why: A 26% fall times an elasticity of −0.13 is a rise of $0.26 \times 0.13 = 3.4\%$; with −0.20 it would be 5.2%. The figures are an illustration in the spirit of Vogel's estimates.

blocks.md: **Result 2:** fitted on 1963–1987 and predicted out of sample, the model with the minimum wage tracks the later college premium better: changes in the real minimum help resolve the puzzle of slowing relative demand, so less slowdown in skill-biased technical change is needed.

blocks.src: assets/Attachments/Vogel 2025 - predicted college premium with and without the minimum wage.png
blocks.alt: Vogel 2025 - predicted college premium with and without the minimum wage

blocks.md: How can the college premium respond so much when few workers earn the minimum and spillovers are small (as AMS find)? Vogel's job-ladder model: on impact the elasticity is small (the direct effect), and over time it grows (the indirect effect as workers move up the ladder). State-level evidence matches: "magnification elasticities" grow over the years after a change.

blocks.src: assets/Attachments/Vogel 2025 - time-varying magnification elasticities.png
blocks.alt: Vogel 2025 - time-varying magnification elasticities

sections.heading: What to be able to do

blocks.md:
1. Explain what DFL's counterfactual densities show and which assumptions they need.
2. State Lee's identifying assumption, write his regression, and compute the marginal effect of the effective minimum $\beta + 2\gamma\, mw$.
3. Explain why measurement error in the median biases OLS estimates of minimum-wage effects, especially far from the median, and how AMS's instrument fixes it.
4. Compute the share of a change in inequality explained by the minimum wage from counterfactual changes.
5. Explain how a uniform national minimum generates variation in its bite across regions, in the US and Brazil.
6. Use elasticities to compute the effect of a change in the real minimum on the college premium, and explain why the effect can grow over time.
